meta.theme: writing defended as a technology rather than a transcription, with the usual argument from punctuation conceded to the other side and the case relocated to the one thing writing removes, the situation in which a speaker can be interrupted and can repair, so that the independence claimed is functional rather than material

meta.reviewer_notes: A genuine dialectic: claim, objection, a reply that the author accepts, and then the objection restated on ground the reply cannot reach. The third paragraph is the hardest thing in the passage, because the author argues on behalf of the view he is attacking and means it, which makes both the withdrawal reading and the preparation reading available for the function question.
meta.tone: argumentative, scrupulous, deliberately modest at the close

quality.adversarial_review: Q1's live rival is the option that the third paragraph withdraws the preceding objection, which a reader forms from the words granting it costs the objection its most quotable example; what is surrendered there is one example, and the following paragraph reopens the attack with the words what the concession does not cover, so nothing was withdrawn. Q2's rival is the option about describing devices that speech never needed, which is the second paragraph's content offered as the purpose of the whole; the passage concedes that line of argument in the third paragraph and would be self-defeating if that were its purpose. Q3's rival is the option that a listener could follow written prose if it were read aloud with care, which the closing test contradicts by asking whether a listener could have held the clauses open to the end with no opportunity to ask. Q4's rival is the option about remaining legible for centuries, which takes survive and author in their commonest senses; the sentence is the last of a paragraph entirely about interruption, repair and the frown of a bewildered hearer, so the absence at issue is the absence of the speaker from the reading, not the death of the writer.

paragraphs.text: Linguists have insisted for a century that writing is not language but a record of it: a set of marks standing for sounds, secondary, derivative, and of no more theoretical interest than a photograph is to a face. The insistence protects something worth protecting. Speech is acquired without instruction, is universal among human communities, and changes of its own accord; writing is taught, is recent, and for most of its history has belonged to a minority. Put the two on a level and the science loses its object. On this account the alphabet is a transcription, and its virtues are a transcription's virtues: fidelity, economy, and the possibility of getting back what went in.

The trouble is that a claim about what writing is has been defended by an argument about what writing was for, and the correspondence, looked at closely, fails in both directions. Punctuation answers to nothing audible in particular, and a comma is not a pause, as anyone can confirm who has followed a text while listening to a recording of it. Spelling preserves distinctions the voice gave up generations ago and manufactures others it never had. The space between words, the most useful device on the page, corresponds to nothing whatever in the stream of sound, which arrives unbroken.

The defender of the older view has a good answer to this and it should be heard. Punctuation and spacing do not transcribe sounds; they transcribe structure, and the structure is genuinely present in the utterance, carried by a speaker in ways no microphone registers. A comma marks a boundary the listener recovers from intonation, from the shape of the clause, from the grammar itself. On this account the page adds nothing to speech. It encodes by visible means what the ear takes from other signals, which is what a good transcription ought to do. So much should be granted, and granting it costs the objection its most quotable example.

What the concession does not cover is the one thing writing takes away. A speaker is interrupted, answered, watched for signs of bewilderment, and can repair a sentence halfway through on the evidence of a frown. A writer has none of this and must anticipate the whole of it in advance. The devices that written prose has grown over centuries are answers to that predicament and to no other: the paragraph, the subordinate clause sustained across three lines, the reference back by name where a voice would be content with a pronoun, the note at the foot of the page that meets an objection nobody has yet made. None of these renders anything a speaker does. They are what a sentence needs when it must survive without its author.

That is a modest conclusion and it had better be kept modest. Nothing here revives the old romance in which literacy remakes the mind of whoever acquires it, and nothing demotes speech, since the technology borrows a grammar and a vocabulary it did not invent and could not replace. The independence is functional rather than material. Writing uses the same language and is still a different instrument, because the problems it exists to solve are problems a speaker never has. The practical test is not whether a written sentence can be read aloud, since nearly all of them can, but whether it could have been said: whether a listener could have held its clauses open to the end with no opportunity to ask.

questions.target_mistake: reading a paragraph that grants the other side one good answer as a withdrawal of the objection itself
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: this paragraph argues the other side's case for it, and gives up one example without giving up the attack.
questions.stem: The third paragraph functions chiefly to

options.A: allow the rival account its strongest reply and concede that one line of attack on it fails
options.B: withdraw the previous paragraph's objection as one the evidence had never supported
options.C: trace the invention of punctuation and spacing by readers rather than by speakers
options.D: raise a second objection to the same account, drawn this time from spelling rather than punctuation

explanation.expert_notice: The paragraph is written from the other side. It opens by saying the defender has a good answer which should be heard, states that answer in full, and closes by saying so much should be granted. The last clause then measures exactly what the grant costs: the objection's most quotable example, not the objection.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option names both halves of the job. The author argues the opposing case properly, which is why punctuation and spacing are said to encode structure rather than sound, and he then accepts that argument. What he accepts is bounded in the final clause, and the next paragraph confirms the bound by opening on what the concession does not cover, which would be an odd sentence to write if the concession had settled anything.
explanation.question_type_note: A paragraph-function question asks what the paragraph is doing for the argument. Where an author states an opponent's answer in the opponent's best form, the paragraph is a concession, and the thing to measure is its size.
explanation.reading_habit: When a paragraph begins by praising an opponent's reply, read to the end of it for the word that measures the concession. Authors who concede an example rarely concede the case, and the measuring word is where they say which they have done.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph surrenders an example and says so: granting the answer costs the objection its most quotable example. The objection itself is restated and pressed in the paragraph that follows, which begins by naming what the concession does not cover.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because a reader who has watched the author argue the other side for five sentences expects a retraction, and the sentence about granting really is the passage's most generous one.

distractors.why_wrong: No history of either device is given anywhere in the passage. Punctuation and spacing appear twice, as marks without audible originals and then as encodings of structure, and neither treatment says who devised them or when.
distractors.seductive_element: The paragraph is about what punctuation does for a reader, which makes a claim about readers having invented it sound like something the passage has already implied.

distractors.why_wrong: Spelling is real passage material in the wrong place. It belongs to the second paragraph, as part of the objection, and the third paragraph raises no objection at all, since its whole business is to answer one.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does argue from spelling, and a reader who remembers the argument without remembering which paragraph held it will accept a second objection as the natural next move.

questions.target_mistake: naming as the purpose the argument from unmatched marks, which the author states in order to give it away
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: the author is moving the case for writing's distinctness off the marks and onto what writing has to do without.
questions.stem: The author's chief purpose in the passage is to

options.A: defend the linguists' insistence that speech, and not writing, is the science's proper object
options.B: relocate the case for writing's independence from the marks it uses to the problems it solves
options.C: describe the devices that written language developed and that spoken language never needed
options.D: warn against the belief that acquiring literacy alters the mind of the person who acquires it

explanation.expert_notice: Two arguments for the same conclusion are offered and one is dropped. The marks argument runs through the second paragraph and is conceded in the third; the fourth then starts again from a different place, the absence of the interruption and the frown, and the fifth calls the independence functional rather than material.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option describes that movement. The conclusion never changes, since the author holds throughout that writing is an instrument in its own right, but the ground shifts from the marks on the page, which he gives away, to the predicament the writer is in, which the defender's reply leaves untouched. The phrase functional rather than material is the author's own summary of the relocation.
explanation.question_type_note: Purpose is a verb with an object. Where a passage argues for one conclusion twice, the purpose lives in the second argument, since the first has been surrendered in front of the reader.
explanation.reading_habit: Ask which of a passage's arguments the author would still hold if the paragraph he concedes were deleted. Purpose questions are decided by the argument that survives the author's own generosity.

distractors.why_wrong: That insistence is the position the passage sets out in order to press against, and the author accepts only a part of it, saying that nothing demotes speech. Accepting part of a view is not writing in order to defend it.
distractors.seductive_element: The first paragraph states the linguists' case sympathetically and says the insistence protects something worth protecting, which reads like endorsement to anyone who stops there.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the second paragraph offered as the whole. The third paragraph takes that argument away, explaining that the devices encode a structure speech carries by other signals, so a passage written for this purpose would have refuted itself halfway through.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the list of unmatched marks is the passage's most concrete material and the easiest part to remember.

distractors.why_wrong: The romance about literacy remaking the mind appears once, in a sentence disclaiming it, and nothing in the argument is built for or against it. A single clause of self-limitation is not what a passage is for.
distractors.seductive_element: The disclaimer sits in the closing paragraph, where readers expect the point to be, and it is the one sentence in the passage that names a famous controversy.

questions.target_mistake: keeping the author's conclusion about writing while dropping the condition that produced it, the absence of a reader who can interrupt
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the inference will restore the missing situation and ask what becomes of the devices when the writer can be questioned.
questions.stem: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?

options.A: a listener could follow written prose as easily as a reader if it were read aloud with care
options.B: spelling ought to be revised whenever the pronunciation it once recorded has changed
options.C: no argument of any complexity can be conducted in a community that has never written
options.D: writing addressed to a reader who can question its writer at once has less need of those devices

explanation.expert_notice: The fourth paragraph states a cause and then a list of effects. The cause is that a writer cannot be interrupted, answered or watched, and must anticipate all of it; the effects are the paragraph, the long subordinate clause, the naming instead of the pronoun, the footnote. The paragraph says these answer that predicament and no other.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option removes the cause and follows the effects down. If the devices exist because the writer is absent when the sentence is read, then writing in which the writer is present and can be asked is writing under a milder version of the predicament, and needs less of the apparatus built for it. Nothing further is claimed: not that such writing is better, and not that the devices would disappear.
explanation.question_type_note: An inference question rewards taking the author's own causal claim and varying the cause. Where a passage says a set of devices answers one predicament and no other, the safe inference concerns what happens when the predicament weakens.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author explains a feature by a condition, ask what the feature would look like without the condition. That question generates the supported inference; options that keep the condition and change the verdict are generating opinions instead.

distractors.why_wrong: The closing test says the reverse. It asks whether a listener could have held the clauses of a written sentence open to the end with no opportunity to ask, and treats the answer as the mark of prose that could not have been spoken.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the same sentence concedes that nearly all written sentences can be read aloud, and a reader who takes reading aloud as the test will find this confirmed.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage reports that spelling preserves distinctions the voice gave up and invents others, and uses the fact as evidence that the marks do not match the sounds. No recommendation about reforming anything is made or implied.
distractors.seductive_element: A mismatch described in a critical tone reads as a defect, and readers supply the repair that a complaint usually carries.

distractors.why_wrong: The fifth paragraph refuses exactly this, saying that nothing here revives the old romance in which literacy remakes the mind. The claim is about what writing must solve, not about what its absence forbids anyone to think.
distractors.seductive_element: The list of devices for sustaining a long argument on the page makes the conclusion about unwritten argument look like the next step.

questions.target_mistake: reading survive and author in their commonest senses, so that the phrase becomes a claim about durability after the writer's death
questions.prediction_target: The learner should paraphrase the phrase from its own paragraph before looking: the sentence must work with nobody there to be asked.
questions.stem: In saying that written devices are what a sentence needs when it must survive without its author, the writer chiefly means that such a sentence must

options.A: remain legible for centuries after the person who composed it is dead and gone
options.B: be understood by readers in places and ages its writer could know nothing about
options.C: manage without the repairs and answers a speaker can supply on being questioned
options.D: say plainly what a speaker would leave to gesture, expression and tone of voice

explanation.expert_notice: The phrase is the last clause of a paragraph about nothing but interruption. Its four preceding sentences describe a speaker being answered, watched for bewilderment and repairing a sentence on the evidence of a frown, and a writer who has none of that. The working definition is planted in front of the phrase, not in the dictionary.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that paragraph in shorter words. Surviving without the author means working while the author is not there to be applied to, which is the condition the paragraph has just spent four sentences describing, and the devices listed are each a substitute for something a present speaker would have done on request. The reading that fits is about the moment of reading, not about a span of years.
explanation.question_type_note: A phrase-in-context question is decided by the sentences around the phrase rather than by the commonest sense of its words. Paraphrase it from its own paragraph before any option is read.
explanation.reading_habit: When a phrase closes a paragraph, treat the paragraph as its definition. Authors put the working sense in the sentences that lead up to a formulation, which is why the option built from the dictionary usually fails.

distractors.why_wrong: Both words are being read in their ordinary senses, and the paragraph supports neither. Nothing in it concerns time, decay or endurance; the absence it describes is the absence of anyone to ask, which is present at every reading whether the writer is alive or not.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because survive and author almost always carry these senses together, and the passage's first paragraph does discuss writing as a record that outlasts the moment.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph asks for anticipation of one reader's misunderstandings, not for intelligibility across cultures and centuries. That would be a claim about the reach of writing, where the passage is making a claim about the absence of a hearer.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like a more sophisticated version of the same idea, and readers reward an option that generalises what they have understood.

distractors.why_wrong: Gesture, expression and tone are never mentioned. The passage's list of what a speaker has is a list of responses to the listener, and the third paragraph has already granted that intonation and clause shape are encoded on the page rather than lost.
distractors.seductive_element: Everyone believes writing lacks tone of voice, and the belief is true enough that the absence of any sentence saying so goes unnoticed.

vocabulary.passage_use: a set of marks standing for sounds, secondary, derivative
vocabulary.meaning_here: taken from something else and having no standing of its own
a written record that sets down something already said

vocabulary.passage_use: What the concession does not cover
vocabulary.meaning_here: a point granted to the other side in an argument

vocabulary.passage_use: answers to that predicament and to no other
vocabulary.meaning_here: the awkward position a writer is placed in by the reader's absence

mentor.challenge: The author spends a whole paragraph arguing for the view he is attacking, and means every word of it. Work out exactly how much he gives away there, because the rest of the passage depends on the size of the gift.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: The familiar argument that writing must be more than a transcription because its marks have no audible originals is conceded to the other side, since punctuation and spacing encode a structure speech really carries, and the case for writing's independence is then rebuilt on the one thing writing removes, a hearer who can interrupt, answer and be repaired to, which makes writing a different instrument functionally without making it a different language.
mentor.main_idea: Writing is usually called a record of speech. One argument against this points to marks with no originals in sound, and the author gives that argument away, because punctuation and spacing encode structure the speaker really carries. What survives is that writing removes the situation: nobody interrupts, nobody frowns, nobody can be asked. The devices of written prose are answers to that, which makes writing a distinct technology without making it independent of the language it borrows.
mentor.simple_explanation:
For about a hundred years linguists have said that writing is not really language. It is just a record of language, the way a photograph is a record of a face. Speech comes first: children pick it up without being taught, every community has it, and it changes by itself. Writing has to be taught, it is recent, and for most of history only a few people had it.

Someone objects. Look at the page, they say. A comma is not a pause; if you follow a text while listening to a recording, the commas and the pauses do not line up. Spelling keeps differences that speakers stopped making long ago. And the gaps between words match nothing at all, because speech arrives as one unbroken stream. So how can this be a transcription, when its most typical marks have nothing to transcribe?

Now comes the interesting move. The author says the other side has a good answer to that, and he gives it in full. Punctuation and spacing are not copying sounds; they are copying structure. The structure really is in the spoken sentence, carried by intonation and by the grammar itself, even if a microphone cannot pick it out. So the page is not inventing anything. It is writing down, with visible marks, what a listener's ear works out from other clues. Fine, says the author. Granted. And with that he loses his best example.

But he has a second argument, and the answer above does not touch it. Think about what writing takes away. A speaker gets interrupted, gets asked to repeat, watches a listener's face and fixes the sentence halfway through when the face goes blank. A writer gets none of that and has to guess all of it in advance. So look at what written prose has built: paragraphs, long sentences that stay open for three lines, saying a name again where a speaker would just say she, footnotes that answer objections nobody has raised yet. None of those is copying anything a speaker does. They are the tools you need when the sentence has to work with nobody there to be asked.

The author then keeps the conclusion small. He is not saying literacy changes your mind, and he is not saying speech is second-rate, because writing borrows a whole grammar and vocabulary it never invented. He is saying writing is a different instrument because it has different problems. His test is nice: not whether a written sentence can be read out loud, since almost all of them can, but whether it could have been said, with a real listener holding all those clauses open and no chance to ask a question.
mentor.why_difficult: The third paragraph is written against the author's own interest, and readers cannot tell how far he has gone. He states the other side's reply, calls it good, and grants it, which looks like surrender until the next paragraph reopens the attack from a different direction. The second difficulty is that two arguments are offered for one conclusion, so a reader who remembers the vivid one, the commas and the spaces, ends up holding the argument the author has thrown away and describing it as the point of the passage. The last paragraph then shrinks the claim twice, once by disclaiming the famous view about literacy and once by calling the independence functional rather than material, and both shrinkages are easy to read past.
mentor.author_intention: To take a popular argument away from his own side, so that the conclusion he wants rests on the fact about writing that no reply can reach: the reader cannot ask, and the sentence must be built to allow for it.

paragraph_journey.note: Writing is a record of speech, and saying so protects something real: speech is learned without teaching and is universal, while writing is taught and recent.
The marks do not match the sounds. Commas are not pauses, spelling keeps what the voice dropped, and the spaces between words match nothing in the stream of speech.
The other side answers that those marks copy structure rather than sound, and the structure really is in the utterance. The author grants it and loses his best example.
What writing removes is the hearer. Nobody interrupts, frowns or asks, so the devices of prose are all answers to a sentence having to work with nobody there.
No claim that literacy remakes minds, and no demotion of speech. A different instrument with the same language, tested by whether a sentence could have been said.

mentor.tone_progression: It opens respectfully towards the view it will press against, sharpens into objection, becomes genuinely fair-minded while arguing the other side's case, gathers force through the paragraph on interruption and repair, and closes deliberately small, disclaiming two larger conclusions the argument might have been used for.
key_transitions: 'The trouble is that a claim about what writing is has been defended by an argument about what writing was for' (opening of paragraph 2): the objection is aimed at the form of the defence rather than at the conclusion.
'So much should be granted, and granting it costs the objection its most quotable example.' (close of paragraph 3): the concession is made and measured in the same sentence.
'What the concession does not cover is the one thing writing takes away.' (opening of paragraph 4): the argument is rebuilt on ground the reply cannot reach.
mentor.misunderstanding: The common wrong model is that the passage proves writing is more than transcription because its marks have no audible originals. That is the argument the author surrenders, in a paragraph most readers experience as a digression rather than as a concession, and a reader who keeps it will answer the purpose question with the second paragraph and the function question with a withdrawal. The opposite error also occurs: a reader who feels the force of the concession decides the author has changed sides, and then cannot account for the paragraph about interruption at all.
mentor.traps_summary: The set offers a concession read as a retraction, the conceded argument offered as the purpose of the passage, a disclaimed view offered as an inference, and the everyday senses of survive and author in place of the ones the paragraph builds. Each is answered by asking which paragraph a claim belongs to and whether the author was still holding it by the end.
mentor.reading_lesson: When an author argues his opponent's case for him, do not read it as a change of mind until you have found the sentence that measures the concession. Good arguers give away an example to keep a claim, and the words that do the measuring, costs the objection its most quotable example, are the ones the questions will be built on. Carry the same habit into purpose questions: the argument an author surrenders in front of you is never what the passage is for.
mentor.real_world: The same shape appears whenever a tool is described as a copy of something older: an email as a letter, a recording as a performance, a spreadsheet as a ledger. In each case the interesting question is not what the new thing reproduces but which part of the old situation it has removed, and what had to be invented to cover the loss.
mentor.takeaway: A written sentence is built for a reader who cannot put up a hand, and almost everything odd about written prose is a reply to that.
mentor.reflection_question: Which habits of your own writing exist only because the reader will not be there to ask you what you meant?

eli10.big_idea: Writing is a different tool from speech, not because of its marks, but because no reader can stop the writer to ask.
eli10.story: Language experts have long said writing is just a record of speech, like a photo of a face. They have a reason: children learn to speak without lessons, but writing must be taught. Some object that writing has things speech lacks. A comma is not a pause. The spaces between words match nothing you hear. The writer admits the experts answer this well. Commas and spaces show a sentence's shape, and speech really has that shape too. So that objection fails. But writing does take one thing away: the listener. Explain a game to a friend, and if she frowns, you try again. A note left on the table cannot see her frown. So a writer must answer every question in advance. Paragraphs, long careful sentences and footnotes exist for this. Writing uses the same language, yet it is a different tool. That does not make speech less important.
paragraphs: States the experts' view: writing is just a record of speech, and gives their good reason.
Raises an objection: commas, spelling and spaces between words match nothing you can hear.
Grants the other side's reply: these marks show a sentence's shape, which speech really has.
Moves the case: writing removes the listener who can interrupt, and its tools answer that problem.
Keeps the claim small: writing does not remake minds or outrank speech; it is a different tool.
eli10.author_view: The writer is fair to the other side, gives up a weak argument willingly, and is careful not to claim too much.
